title: HashSet internals: backed by HashMap, dummy PRESENT value
keyPoints: HashSet is a wrapper around HashMap; internally it holds a HashMap<E, Object> where each element is a key and the value is a shared dummy constant called PRESENT
add(e) calls map.put(e, PRESENT) and returns true if the key was new (put returned null), false if it already existed
contains(e) delegates to map.containsKey(e); remove(e) delegates to map.remove(e); all operations are O(1) average
All HashMap properties are inherited: default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, treeification at 8 collisions, allows one null element
Elements must implement proper hashCode() and equals() because they serve as HashMap keys
LinkedHashSet wraps LinkedHashMap (insertion order); TreeSet wraps TreeMap (sorted order) – the same pattern
Memory overhead is ~32-48 bytes per element due to the HashMap Node wrapper

s1_definition.oneliner: HashSet is a HashMap in disguise: each element is a key in the HashMap, and every value is the same shared dummy constant PRESENT.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Internal structure**: `private transient HashMap<E, Object> map` – a plain HashMap
- **Dummy value**: `private static final Object PRESENT = new Object()` – one object shared by all entries
- **add(e)**: calls `map.put(e, PRESENT)` and returns true if put returned null (new key), false if key already existed
- **contains(e)**: calls `map.containsKey(e)` – O(1) hash lookup
- **remove(e)**: calls `map.remove(e)` – O(1) hash lookup
- All HashMap properties are inherited: capacity, load factor, treeification, null handling
s1_definition.analogy: HashSet is like a filing cabinet (HashMap) where every drawer has a label (your element as the key) and inside every drawer is the same rubber stamp saying "PRESENT" (the dummy value). You only care about the drawer labels – the set elements. Adding a duplicate label? HashMap says "this key already exists," so HashSet says "rejected."

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  HashSet = HashMap wrapper

  HashSet<String>:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ HashMap<String, Object>                  │
  │                                          │
  │ Bucket 2: ["SAV2001" → PRESENT]          │
  │ Bucket 5: ["CUR3001" → PRESENT]          │
  │ Bucket 9: ["FD4001" → PRESENT]           │
  │                                          │
  │ PRESENT = new Object()  (shared by all)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  add("SAV2001") → map.put("SAV2001", PRESENT)
                 → put returns null (new key)
                 → add returns true

  add("SAV2001") → map.put("SAV2001", PRESENT)
                 → put returns PRESENT (existing)
                 → add returns false (duplicate!)

  Same pattern:
  LinkedHashSet → LinkedHashMap (insertion order)
  TreeSet       → TreeMap (sorted order)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HashSet is one of the simplest classes in the JDK to understand once you know the secret: it is just a HashMap wrapper. Every element you add becomes a key in an internal HashMap, with a shared dummy PRESENT object as the value. add() delegates to put(), contains() delegates to containsKey(), and remove() delegates to remove(). All the HashMap properties – O(1) operations, default capacity 16, load factor 0.75, treeification at 8 collisions – apply to HashSet automatically.

In the National Bank of India's fraud detection system, Rajesh uses HashSet to maintain the set of blocked account numbers. When a transfer request arrives, `blockedAccounts.contains(sourceAccount)` answers in O(1) time. Using an ArrayList for this check would scan all 50,000 blocked accounts on every transfer – thousands of times slower.

The critical requirement is that elements must implement proper hashCode() and equals(). Without these, two logically identical objects are treated as different set members, allowing duplicates to sneak in.

Remember one sentence: HashSet is a HashMap where elements are keys and values are a shared dummy constant, so all HashMap behavior – hashing, buckets, collisions – applies to HashSet.
